title: How reinforcement learning after next-token prediction facilitates learning
claim: Reinforcement learning after next-token prediction unlocks generalization and longer responses that pre-training alone cannot achieve on a hard task.
layout: 2 halves: left pipeline diagram, right stacked accuracy/length plots with zoom insets
description: The left half shows the learning setup. At the top, a data distribution has short sequences (bits x1..xd, then the parity product, then EOS, probability 1-p_cot) and long sequences (bits, then chain-of-thought partial products, parity, EOS, probability p_cot). They use blue, yellow and red blocks. Below, a green stacked-card pipeline shows next-token pre-training: training data goes into a Transformer, which produces inference samples with red X marks on errors. A reward arrow then feeds a reinforcement-learning post-training loop, where Transformer and inference cards repeat over RL iterations until the outputs are correct. The right half has two stacked line plots. The top plot shows accuracy plateauing near 50% for the red pre-training curve, then jumping to 100% in blue when post-training starts at 5k, 10k and 20k iterations. The bottom plot shows median response length jumping from 1 to 50 after post-training starts. Each plot has a zoom inset.
caption: Left: An illustration of our main learning setting: a mixture of long and short sequences encoding the parity of $d$ bits, along with a representation of pre-training and post-training for $d$=5. Right: Advantage of next-token prediction followed by reinforcement learning over mere next-token prediction in predicting the parity of $d$=50 bits with a transformer trained from scratch. The red line corresponds to pre-training using next-token prediction, while blue lines correspond to the same pre-training runs, each followed by GRPO (with a final token accuracy reward) from a different checkpoint. Lines correspond to median across 3 seeds. Top: Test accuracy under greedy decoding. Bottom: Median length of model response under greedy decoding. The inset figures zoom-in on the curves during post-training. Accuracy plateaus around 50% (random guess) during pre-training and then immediately grows during post-training. Also, length increases during post-training.
abstract: Recent advances in reasoning domains with neural networks have primarily been enabled by a training recipe that optimizes Large Language Models, previously trained to predict the next-token in a sequence, with reinforcement learning algorithms. We introduce a framework to study the success of this paradigm, and we theoretically expose the optimization mechanisms by which reinforcement learning improves over next-token prediction in this setting. We study learning from mixture distributions of short and long ``chain-of-thought'' sequences encoding a single task. In particular, when the task consists of predicting the parity of $d$ bits and long sequences are rare, we show how reinforcement learning after next-token prediction enables autoregressive transformers to generalize, whereas mere next-token prediction requires extreme statistical or computational resources to do so. We further explain how reinforcement learning leverages increased test-time computation, manifested in longer responses, to facilitate this learning process. In a simplified setting, we theoretically prove that autoregressive linear models following this training recipe can efficiently learn to predict the parity of $d$ bits as long as the proportion of long demonstrations in the data mix is not exponentially small in the input dimension $d$. Finally, we demonstrate these same phenomena in other settings, including the post-training of Llama-series models on mixture variations of common mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
